# KMS and CloudHSM: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=kms-q004 -->
### Question 1

A company stores many terabytes of objects in Amazon S3. The objects are encrypted with a symmetric customer managed AWS KMS key, and the security team wrote its own key policy for that key. A new company policy requires the company to rotate the key material every year. The security team must keep control of the key policy. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a new customer managed key every year, re-encrypt all objects in the bucket under the new key, and then schedule the old key for deletion.
- Enable automatic key rotation on the customer managed key, and keep the existing key policy and the key ID that the applications already use.
- Run a scheduled AWS Lambda function every year that copies each object onto itself, so that Amazon S3 encrypts every object under new data keys.
- Switch the encryption of the bucket to the AWS managed key for Amazon S3, because AWS rotates the key material of that key every year.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Enable automatic key rotation on the customer managed key, and keep the existing key policy and the key ID that the applications already use.

**Deciding phrases.** "many terabytes", "symmetric customer managed AWS KMS key", "rotate the key material every year", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
2. I mark the constraints: a symmetric customer managed key, many terabytes in Amazon S3, new key material every year, and the security team keeps its own key policy.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict automatic key rotation, because AWS KMS can rotate the key material of a symmetric customer managed key and keep the same key.
4. I remove the AWS managed key, because the team cannot change its key policy. I remove the yearly copy of the objects, because new data keys do not give the KMS key new key material.
5. Between automatic rotation and a new key with a full re-encryption, the difference is the work; the stem says many terabytes and LEAST operational overhead, and KMS keeps the old key material to decrypt old objects, so nothing needs re-encryption.
6. Check: automatic rotation gives new key material every year, keeps the key policy and the key ID, and moves no data. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** Automatic rotation is the built-in answer for a symmetric customer managed key. KMS [keeps previous versions of keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-faq-auto-rotation-no-reencrypt) to decrypt old objects and encrypts new requests under the newest version. The key stays [the same logical resource](../facts/kms.md#kms-rotation-same-logical-key-transparent), so the key policy, the key ID and the applications stay as they are.

**Why not.**

- "Create a new customer managed key every year, ...": It works, but KMS [keeps previous versions of keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-faq-auto-rotation-no-reencrypt) to decrypt old data, so the yearly re-encryption of many terabytes is work that rotation does not need.
- "Run a scheduled AWS Lambda function every year ...": New data keys are not new KMS key material. Key rotation [changes only the current key material](../facts/kms.md#kms-rotation-same-logical-key-transparent) of the KMS key, and this function does not touch it.
- "Switch the encryption of the bucket to the ...": The key would rotate, but the team would lose its own key policy, because you [cannot change any properties of AWS managed keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-aws-managed-key-cannot-change).

**Twin.** If the stem said "an asymmetric RSA key that signs documents" instead: create a new key and move the alias, because [automatic key rotation is not supported](../facts/kms.md#kms-faq-asym-hmac-no-auto-rotation-alias) for asymmetric keys.

**Takeaway.** A yearly rotation rule on a symmetric customer managed key: enable automatic rotation, and re-encrypt nothing.

**Review.** [Automatic rotation changes only the key material and keeps the same KMS key](2-deep.md#automatic-rotation-changes-only-the-key-material-and-keeps-the-same-kms-key-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=kms-q001 -->
### Question 2

A company stores sensitive files in an Amazon S3 bucket that uses server-side encryption with a customer managed AWS KMS key (SSE-KMS). The key policy allows IAM policies in the account to control access to the key. A new application role has an IAM policy that allows s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on the bucket and allows no KMS actions. The application only downloads existing objects from the bucket. Every request from the application fails with an access denied error. Which change will fix the problem with LEAST privilege?

- Add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the customer managed key that encrypts the bucket.
- Add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows kms:GenerateDataKey on the ARN of the customer managed key that encrypts the bucket.
- Add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows every KMS action, kms:*, on every KMS key in the account.
- Replace the S3 statements in the IAM policy of the role with one statement that allows every Amazon S3 action, s3:*, on the bucket.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the customer managed key that encrypts the bucket.

**Deciding phrases.** "only downloads existing objects from the bucket", "allows no KMS actions", "LEAST privilege"

**Why.** SSE-KMS puts a KMS key between the role and the data. To download an object, the caller needs [kms:Decrypt permissions for the key](../facts/kms.md#kms-s3-sse-kms-put-get-permissions). The key policy already lets IAM policies control access, so one IAM statement is enough. Least privilege means you [specify the key ARN of each KMS key](../facts/kms.md#kms-iam-least-privilege-key-arns) and add one action.

**Why not.**

- "Add a statement to the IAM policy of ...": The application downloads objects. An upload needs [kms:GenerateDataKey permissions on the key](../facts/kms.md#kms-s3-sse-kms-put-get-permissions), but a download needs kms:Decrypt, which this statement leaves out.
- "Add a statement to the IAM policy of ...": It works, but it allows every KMS action on every key, and least privilege gives principals [only the permissions they need](../facts/kms.md#kms-iam-least-privilege-key-arns).
- "Replace the S3 statements in the IAM policy ...": S3 actions do not open the KMS key: no principal, [including the account root user or key creator](../facts/kms.md#kms-no-principal-has-access-unless-allowed), can use a key without an explicit allow.

**Twin.** If the stem said "only uploads new objects in single PUT requests" instead: allow kms:GenerateDataKey, because an upload needs [kms:GenerateDataKey permissions on the key](../facts/kms.md#kms-s3-sse-kms-put-get-permissions).

**Takeaway.** With SSE-KMS, a download also needs kms:Decrypt on the key, and an upload needs kms:GenerateDataKey.

**Review.** [IAM policies and other accounts count only when the key policy allows them](2-deep.md#iam-policies-and-other-accounts-count-only-when-the-key-policy-allows-them-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A media company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances that creates large video files. Company policy requires that each file is encrypted at rest with a key that the security team controls in AWS KMS. The application must encrypt each file itself before it stores the file in Amazon S3. Later, other authorized applications must be able to decrypt each file. What should the application do for each file?

- Call the Encrypt operation with the KMS key and the whole video file as the plaintext, and store the ciphertext that AWS KMS returns in Amazon S3.
- Download the key material of the KMS key to the application, encrypt the file locally with that key material, and store the file in Amazon S3.
- Call GenerateDataKey with the KMS key, encrypt the file locally with the plaintext data key, and store the encrypted data key with the encrypted file.
- Call GenerateDataKey with the KMS key, encrypt the file locally with the plaintext data key, and store the plaintext data key with the encrypted file.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Call GenerateDataKey with the KMS key, encrypt the file locally with the plaintext data key, and store the encrypted data key with the encrypted file.

**Deciding phrases.** "large video files", "encrypt each file itself", "able to decrypt each file"

**Why.** This pattern is envelope encryption. A KMS key protects a small data key, and the data key encrypts the large file outside AWS KMS. After use, the application should [remove it from memory as soon as possible](../facts/kms.md#kms-envelope-store-encrypted-data-key). Later, the encrypted data key can be [decrypted by only users with permissions](../facts/kms.md#kms-faq-exported-data-key-encrypted-under-kms-key) to use the KMS key.

**Why not.**

- "Call the Encrypt operation with the KMS key ...": The Encrypt operation takes plaintext of up to [4,096 bytes](../facts/kms.md#kms-encrypt-max-plaintext-4096-bytes), so a whole video file cannot go to AWS KMS directly.
- "Download the key material of the KMS key ...": KMS keys [never leave the service unencrypted](../facts/kms.md#kms-keys-never-leave-unencrypted), so the application cannot download the key material of a KMS key.
- "Call GenerateDataKey with the KMS key, encrypt the ...": A plaintext data key beside the file lets anyone who reads the file decrypt it. AWS says to [safely store the encrypted data key](../facts/kms.md#kms-envelope-store-encrypted-data-key) with the data.

**Twin.** If the stem said "short secrets of a few hundred bytes" instead: the Encrypt operation also works, because it encrypts plaintext of [up to 4,096 bytes](../facts/kms.md#kms-encrypt-max-plaintext-4096-bytes).

**Takeaway.** Large data: call GenerateDataKey, encrypt locally, and store the encrypted data key with the data.

**Review.** [A KMS key protects a data key and the data key encrypts your data](2-deep.md#a-kms-key-protects-a-data-key-and-the-data-key-encrypts-your-data-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company stores customer orders in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The table uses the default encryption at rest, and no one has changed its encryption settings. A new security rule says that the security team must decide which IAM roles can use the encryption key of the table. The team must also audit each use of that key in AWS CloudTrail. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Switch the encryption of the table to the AWS managed key for DynamoDB, and edit the key policy of that key so that it names the allowed roles.
- Keep the AWS owned key that encrypts the table, and create an AWS CloudTrail trail that records each use of that key in the account.
- Create a key in an AWS CloudHSM key store that the company operates, and switch the encryption of the table to that customer managed key.
- Create a customer managed KMS key with a key policy that names the allowed roles, and switch the encryption of the table to that new key.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a customer managed KMS key with a key policy that names the allowed roles, and switch the encryption of the table to that new key.

**Deciding phrases.** "default encryption at rest", "decide which IAM roles can use the encryption key", "audit each use of that key", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** DynamoDB lets you [switch between these key types at any time](../facts/kms.md#kms-dynamodb-always-encrypted-three-key-types). AWS owned keys [do not provide policy controls or CloudTrail logs](../facts/kms.md#kms-faq-aws-owned-no-policy-no-logs). With a customer managed key, [you have full control over these KMS keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-customer-managed-key-full-control), including the key policy, and the team reads each use in CloudTrail.

**Why not.**

- "Switch the encryption of the table to the ...": The service controls that key policy: you [cannot change any properties of AWS managed keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-aws-managed-key-cannot-change), and the key policy is one of them.
- "Keep the AWS owned key that encrypts the ...": For an AWS owned key, the logging of key use is [not viewable by the customer](../facts/kms.md#kms-key-type-logging-owned-not-viewable), so a new trail shows nothing about that key.
- "Create a key in an AWS CloudHSM key ...": A custom key store brings [additional cost, operational complexity, and reduced performance](../facts/kms.md#kms-custom-key-store-only-if-mandated), and no rule here asks for dedicated HSMs.

**Twin.** If the stem said "must encrypt the data and needs no control or audit of the key" instead: keep the AWS owned key, because it fits unless you are [required to audit or control the encryption key](../facts/kms.md#kms-aws-owned-key-good-choice-unless-audit).

**Takeaway.** Control of the key policy plus an audit trail of each use points to a customer managed key.

**Review.** [The key type decides who controls the key policy and who sees its use](2-deep.md#the-key-type-decides-who-controls-the-key-policy-and-who-sees-its-use-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company stores sensitive files in an Amazon S3 bucket that uses server-side encryption with a customer managed AWS KMS key (SSE-KMS). The key policy allows IAM policies in the account to control access to the key. A new application role has an IAM policy that allows s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on the bucket and allows no KMS actions. The application only uploads new objects in single PUT requests. Every request from the application fails with an access denied error. Which change will fix the problem with LEAST privilege?

- Add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the customer managed key that encrypts the bucket.
- Add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows kms:GenerateDataKey on the ARN of the customer managed key that encrypts the bucket.
- Add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows every KMS action, kms:*, on every KMS key in the account.
- Replace the S3 statements in the IAM policy of the role with one statement that allows every Amazon S3 action, s3:*, on the bucket.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows kms:GenerateDataKey on the ARN of the customer managed key that encrypts the bucket.

**Deciding phrases.** "only uploads new objects in single PUT requests", "allows no KMS actions", "LEAST privilege"

**Why.** SSE-KMS puts a KMS key between the role and the data. To upload an object, the caller needs [kms:GenerateDataKey permissions on the key](../facts/kms.md#kms-s3-sse-kms-put-get-permissions). The key policy already lets IAM policies control access, so one IAM statement is enough. Least privilege means you [specify the key ARN of each KMS key](../facts/kms.md#kms-iam-least-privilege-key-arns) and add one action.

**Why not.**

- "Add a statement to the IAM policy of ...": The application uploads objects. An upload needs [kms:GenerateDataKey permissions on the key](../facts/kms.md#kms-s3-sse-kms-put-get-permissions), and kms:Decrypt is the permission for downloads.
- "Add a statement to the IAM policy of ...": It works, but it allows every KMS action on every key, and least privilege gives principals [only the permissions they need](../facts/kms.md#kms-iam-least-privilege-key-arns).
- "Replace the S3 statements in the IAM policy ...": S3 actions do not open the KMS key: no principal, [including the account root user or key creator](../facts/kms.md#kms-no-principal-has-access-unless-allowed), can use a key without an explicit allow.

**Twin.** If the stem said "only downloads existing objects from the bucket" instead: allow kms:Decrypt, because a download needs [kms:Decrypt permissions for the key](../facts/kms.md#kms-s3-sse-kms-put-get-permissions).

**Takeaway.** With SSE-KMS, an upload also needs kms:GenerateDataKey on the key, and a download needs kms:Decrypt.

### Question 6

A company has two AWS accounts in an organization in AWS Organizations. Account A owns a customer managed AWS KMS key that encrypts files in an Amazon S3 bucket. An application in account B runs with an IAM role and must decrypt data that is encrypted under this key. The key policy names only principals in account A. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with LEAST privilege? (Select TWO.)

- In account B, attach a service control policy (SCP) to the account that allows kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the key in account A.
- In account A, add a statement to the key policy that allows kms:Decrypt for the ARN of the IAM role of the application in account B.
- In account B, add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows kms:Decrypt with the wildcard character as the resource, so every key matches.
- In account B, add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the customer managed key in account A.
- In account A, re-encrypt the files under the AWS managed key for Amazon S3, and share that AWS managed key with account B.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- In account A, add a statement to the key policy that allows kms:Decrypt for the ARN of the IAM role of the application in account B.
- In account B, add a statement to the IAM policy of the role that allows kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the customer managed key in account A.

**Deciding phrases.** "Account A owns a customer managed AWS KMS key", "An application in account B", "LEAST privilege"

**Why.** The key and the role are in different accounts. Cross-account use of a key requires [permission in the key policy](../facts/kms.md#kms-cross-account-key-policy-and-iam-policy) of the key in account A and [an IAM policy in the external user's account](../facts/kms.md#kms-cross-account-key-policy-and-iam-policy) in account B. Each statement names one action and one role or key.

- Across accounts, use of a key requires [permission in the key policy](../facts/kms.md#kms-cross-account-key-policy-and-iam-policy), and this statement names one role and one action.
- Account B also needs [an IAM policy in the external user's account](../facts/kms.md#kms-cross-account-key-policy-and-iam-policy), and this statement names one key ARN and one action.

**Why not.**

- "In account B, attach a service control policy ...": [An SCP never grants permissions](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-never-grants-permissions), so it cannot replace an allow in the IAM policy of the role in account B.
- "In account B, add a statement to the ...": It works together with the key policy statement, but it matches every key, and best practice is to [specify the key ARN of each KMS key](../facts/kms.md#kms-iam-least-privilege-key-arns).
- "In account A, re-encrypt the files under the ...": The service controls the key policy of that key, and you [cannot change any properties of AWS managed keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-aws-managed-key-cannot-change), so account B cannot be added.

**Twin.** If the stem said "an application role in account A" instead: one key policy statement that names the role is enough, because the key policy is [the primary way to control access](../facts/kms.md#kms-key-policy-primary-exactly-one).

**Takeaway.** Cross-account KMS use needs two allows: the key policy in the key's account and an IAM policy in the caller's account.

**Review.** [IAM policies and other accounts count only when the key policy allows them](2-deep.md#iam-policies-and-other-accounts-count-only-when-the-key-policy-allows-them-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A financial services company is moving a Java application to AWS. Regulations require that the application's encryption keys are generated and stored in single-tenant hardware security modules (HSMs) under the company's exclusive control. The application calls its cryptographic library through the Java Cryptography Extension (JCE) interface, and the company does not want to change this code. The keys must stay available if one Availability Zone fails. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create customer managed keys in AWS KMS in the default key store, and allow the application role to use the keys in each key policy.
- Run HSM appliances that the company owns in two of its data centers, and connect them to the VPC through AWS Direct Connect.
- Create an AWS CloudHSM cluster with two HSMs in two Availability Zones, and generate and use the keys through the CloudHSM client libraries.
- Use the AWS managed keys that AWS KMS creates for each service, and limit their use by editing the key policy of each managed key.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an AWS CloudHSM cluster with two HSMs in two Availability Zones, and generate and use the keys through the CloudHSM client libraries.

**Deciding phrases.** "single-tenant hardware security modules (HSMs) under the company's exclusive control", "Java Cryptography Extension (JCE)", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Compared with AWS KMS, CloudHSM gives a [single-tenant HSM cluster](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-vs-kms-faq-single-tenant-vpc-exclusive) with [exclusive control over how your keys are used](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-vs-kms-faq-single-tenant-vpc-exclusive). Its libraries support [Java JCE](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-faq-standard-apis). With [at least two HSMs](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-faq-ha-automatic-two-azs) across two Availability Zones, high availability is automatic.

**Why not.**

- "Create customer managed keys in AWS KMS in ...": AWS KMS has [no native integration](../facts/kms.md#kms-faq-no-native-openssl-jce-cng) with JCE, and compared with KMS, CloudHSM is the service that gives a [single-tenant HSM cluster](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-vs-kms-faq-single-tenant-vpc-exclusive).
- "Run HSM appliances that the company owns in ...": It works, but the company runs hardware and network links itself, and CloudHSM already gives [exclusive control over how your keys are used](../facts/cloudhsm.md#cloudhsm-vs-kms-faq-single-tenant-vpc-exclusive).
- "Use the AWS managed keys that AWS KMS ...": You [cannot change any properties of AWS managed keys](../facts/kms.md#kms-aws-managed-key-cannot-change), so the company can neither edit their key policies nor control them exclusively.

**Twin.** If the stem said "hardware security modules (HSMs) validated at FIPS 140-3 Level 3" instead: a KMS customer managed key, because all KMS keys use HSMs validated under [FIPS 140-3 Security Level 3](../facts/kms.md#kms-hsm-fips-140-3-level-3).

**Takeaway.** Single-tenant HSMs under your exclusive control, or a PKCS #11 or JCE interface, point to AWS CloudHSM.

**Review.** [AWS CloudHSM gives you single-tenant hardware security modules that you operate](2-deep.md#aws-cloudhsm-gives-you-single-tenant-hardware-security-modules-that-you-operate-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A security team created a customer managed AWS KMS key with a custom key policy. The key policy has one statement, which gives full access to the team's administrator role. Developer roles have IAM policies that allow kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the key, but their Decrypt calls fail with an access denied error. From now on, the team wants to centrally manage access to this key with IAM policies, as it does for other resources. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a KMS grant for each developer role that allows kms:Decrypt on the key, and create another grant for every new developer role.
- Attach an IAM policy to the developer roles that allows every KMS action, kms:*, with the wildcard character as the resource of the statement.
- Add a statement to the key policy that allows access for the account principal, so that IAM policies in the account can allow use of the key.
- Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to the developer roles, so that the roles get full access to every resource in the account.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add a statement to the key policy that allows access for the account principal, so that IAM policies in the account can allow use of the key.

**Deciding phrases.** "custom key policy", "IAM policies that allow kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the key", "centrally manage access to this key with IAM policies"

**Why.** A KMS key policy [does not automatically give permission to the account](../facts/kms.md#kms-key-policy-no-automatic-account-permission), so the IAM allows of the developers are ignored. [The default key policy enables IAM policies](../facts/kms.md#kms-iam-policy-allow-needs-key-policy) with a statement for the account principal. Adding that statement turns on IAM-based access, and the team then manages access in IAM.

**Why not.**

- "Create a KMS grant for each developer role ...": It works, but [grants are often used for temporary permissions](../facts/kms.md#kms-grant-allow-only-one-key-temporary), and one grant per role is not central management with IAM.
- "Attach an IAM policy to the developer roles ...": Without permission from the key policy, [IAM policies that allow permissions have no effect](../facts/kms.md#kms-iam-policy-allow-needs-key-policy), even with every action on every resource.
- "Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to the developer ...": AdministratorAccess is an IAM policy too, and without the key policy, [IAM policies that allow permissions have no effect](../facts/kms.md#kms-iam-policy-allow-needs-key-policy) on the key.

**Twin.** If the stem said "one developer role needs access for one day" instead: create a grant, because [grants are often used for temporary permissions](../facts/kms.md#kms-grant-allow-only-one-key-temporary).

**Takeaway.** A KMS key ignores IAM allows until its key policy has the statement for the account principal.

**Review.** [IAM policies and other accounts count only when the key policy allows them](2-deep.md#iam-policies-and-other-accounts-count-only-when-the-key-policy-allows-them-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

An application encrypts data on the client side with a single-Region AWS KMS key in us-east-1. The application replicates the encrypted data to us-west-2 for disaster recovery. During an outage in us-east-1, an application role in us-west-2 must decrypt the replicated data without a cross-Region call to us-east-1. The company accepts a one-time re-encryption of the existing data. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Update the existing single-Region key in us-east-1 so that it becomes a multi-Region key, and create a replica of that key in us-west-2.
- Allow the application role in us-west-2 to use kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the existing key in us-east-1, and call that ARN during the outage.
- Create a new multi-Region primary key in us-east-1, create a replica of it in us-west-2, and encrypt the data under the primary key.
- Create a single-Region key in us-west-2, and run a scheduled job that decrypts each replicated object and re-encrypts it under that key.
- Write a key policy for the replica key in us-west-2 that allows the application role in us-west-2 to use the replica key for decryption.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create a new multi-Region primary key in us-east-1, create a replica of it in us-west-2, and encrypt the data under the primary key.
- Write a key policy for the replica key in us-west-2 that allows the application role in us-west-2 to use the replica key for decryption.

**Deciding phrases.** "single-Region AWS KMS key", "without a cross-Region call to us-east-1", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The recovery Region needs its own key for the data. Related multi-Region keys have [the same key material and key ID](../facts/kms.md#kms-mrk-same-material-no-cross-region-call), so a replica decrypts locally. You [manage each multi-Region key independently](../facts/kms.md#kms-mrk-independent-policies-grants-aliases), so the replica gets its own key policy for the role.

- Related multi-Region keys share [the same key material and key ID](../facts/kms.md#kms-mrk-same-material-no-cross-region-call), so the replica in us-west-2 decrypts the data with no call to us-east-1.
- Each related key keeps its own policy, because you [manage each multi-Region key independently](../facts/kms.md#kms-mrk-independent-policies-grants-aliases), so the replica needs a statement for the role.

**Why not.**

- "Update the existing single-Region key in us-east-1 so ...": The multi-Region property is fixed when a key is created: [you cannot convert a single-Region key](../facts/kms.md#kms-mrk-cannot-convert) to a multi-Region key.
- "Allow the application role in us-west-2 to use ...": A single-Region key is [stored and used only in the Region](../facts/kms.md#kms-single-region-key-stays-in-region) where it was created, so each decryption calls us-east-1 and fails in the outage.
- "Create a single-Region key in us-west-2, and run ...": It works for objects that the job already handled, but it is a job to run, and related multi-Region keys decrypt [without re-encrypting or making a cross-Region call](../facts/kms.md#kms-mrk-same-material-no-cross-region-call).

**Twin.** If the stem said "data in each Region must be decryptable in that Region alone" instead: use single-Region keys, because with them keys in a Region can [decrypt sensitive data only in that Region](../facts/kms.md#kms-mrk-data-residency-harder).

**Takeaway.** Decrypt in a second Region with no cross-Region call: a multi-Region key with a replica that has its own key policy.

**Review.** [A KMS key stays in its Region unless you create a multi-Region key](2-deep.md#a-kms-key-stays-in-its-region-unless-you-create-a-multi-region-key-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=kms-q009 -->
### Question 10

A company encrypts the data of one customer with a dedicated customer managed AWS KMS key. The contract with that customer ends today. The company must stop every cryptographic use of the key as soon as possible. A legal review in 60 days can require the company to read the data again, so the company must make sure that access can be restored. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Schedule the key for deletion with the longest waiting period, and cancel the deletion if the legal review requires access to the data.
- Remove kms:Decrypt and kms:Encrypt from every IAM policy in the account that names the key, and keep the key policy as it is.
- Add a statement to the key policy that denies all cryptographic operations to every principal, and remove that statement after the legal review.
- Disable the key now, and enable the key again later if the legal review requires the company to read the data of the customer.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Disable the key now, and enable the key again later if the legal review requires the company to read the data of the customer.

**Deciding phrases.** "stop every cryptographic use of the key as soon as possible", "A legal review in 60 days", "make sure that access can be restored"

**Why.** Disabling is the reversible switch. AWS suggests [disabling the KMS key instead of deleting it](../facts/kms.md#kms-disable-instead-of-delete) when you are not sure that you no longer need it. A disabled key cannot be used [until you re-enable it](../facts/kms.md#kms-disabled-key-no-crypto-until-reenabled), and enabling it again brings back access to the data.

**Why not.**

- "Schedule the key for deletion with the longest ...": The waiting period is [7 – 30 days](../facts/kms.md#kms-deletion-waiting-period-7-to-30-days), shorter than the review, and after deletion [that data becomes unrecoverable](../facts/kms.md#kms-deletion-irreversible-data-unrecoverable).
- "Remove kms:Decrypt and kms:Encrypt from every IAM policy ...": The key policy is [the primary way to control access](../facts/kms.md#kms-key-policy-primary-exactly-one), and it can still allow principals directly, so IAM changes do not stop every use.
- "Add a statement to the key policy that ...": It works, but the policy edits are extra work: a disabled key is blocked from cryptographic use [until you re-enable it](../facts/kms.md#kms-disabled-key-no-crypto-until-reenabled).

**Twin.** If the stem said "the data must become unreadable for good" instead: schedule the key for deletion, because after deletion [that data becomes unrecoverable](../facts/kms.md#kms-deletion-irreversible-data-unrecoverable).

**Takeaway.** Stop key use with a way back: disable the key. Schedule deletion for data that the company will not read again.

**Review.** [A disabled KMS key can be re-enabled but a deleted one cannot be recovered](2-deep.md#a-disabled-kms-key-can-be-re-enabled-but-a-deleted-one-cannot-be-recovered-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->
